script: I demanded a new gift after family got our names wrong—unbelievable fallout!. I got hitched last year, my wife and I—he's 31, she's 32, just a normal couple. The day was lit: cake, vows, that kind of thing. We got a ton of gifts, all sweet. But one—this personalized cheese board—felt like a slap in the face. The board's supposed to have our names and the wedding date, right? Instead, it's got the wrong date, my name misspelled (and trust me, it's a common name, so you'd think it'd be easy). And to top it off, I am lactose‑intolerant, vegan 99% of the time. My wife is vegan too. So it's basically a useless piece of wood with a typo on it. I told the gift‑giver straight up after the wedding: "Can we do a replacement or return?" No response. A few weeks later, my family visits. I pull the board out, show them the misspelling, the wrong date. I say, "I'd love to display it, but it just… doesn't work." They look at me like I am the villain for asking. "You're being rude," they say. "It's the thought that counts." I am like, "Thought? This is a typo. It's not even usable." I am not even mad about the board itself—if it were a generic one, I'd use it. It's the engraving that kills me. Imagine you're a kid, get a gift that's wrong. It's like getting a birthday cake with the wrong name. It feels like the person didn't even try. Now my family's saying I am being a jerk for demanding a fix. I am not. I am just saying, "I didn't get what I was promised." If they can't fix it, at least let me return it. It's not a big deal—whoever did the engraving didn't know me well enough to get it right. And I've known this person for years. The audacity, right? So, am I the jerk? No. I am just protecting my vibe and the integrity of our wedding day. The board is a reminder of a mistake, and that's not something I want hanging in our home. If they can't correct it, I'll just keep it as a reminder that even the best people can screw up. And that's the tea.
